request.system: You are clustering code review findings from one PR. Always respond with valid JSON.
request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

PAIRS:
PAIR 1:
A: `remove_member` uses `group.users.delete(user_id)` followed by `group.save`, which deletes the join row without executing GroupUser callbacks and does not recompute `group.user_count`. After a successful removal through this endpoint the group's denormalized `user_count` (displayed as `({{user_count}})` in the new admin template and used for pagination via `meta.total`) is stale until something else refreshes it, so the member pagination shows a wrong total and a phantom page.
B: groups_controller#remove_member uses `group.users.delete(user_id)` which skips destroy callbacks, so the user_count counter cache on the group is never decremented, leaving UI user_count and pagination totals stale

PAIR 2:
A: remove_member uses `group.users.delete(user_id)`, which deletes the join row directly and bypasses the Group membership callbacks (user_count maintenance, automatic-group refresh hooks) that Group#remove goes through. After removing a member the group's cached user_count is stale until refresh_automatic_groups/reload; any logic keyed on user_count (visibility checks, 'groups.visible' behavior, admin UI pagination totals) reports a member count that includes the removed user, and any future callback added to Group#remove (e.g. primary-group downgrade) silently never fires for this path.
B: groups_controller#remove_member uses `group.users.delete(user_id)` which skips destroy callbacks, so the user_count counter cache on the group is never decremented, leaving UI user_count and pagination totals stale

PAIR 3:
A: remove_member calls group.users.delete(user_id) then group.save and returns success_json even when the user was never a member, and group.save is a no-op on an unchanged record so validation cannot report the miss. A request with a stale or wrong user_id gets a 200 success while no membership was removed; the admin UI (which reloads the list and trusts the response) treats the no-op as a confirmed removal, hiding the real state from the operator.
B: remove_member silently no-ops (and returns success) when user_id is not a member of the group, and group.save on an untouched record can never fail so the 422 branch is dead. A stale UI or double-invocation sends a user_id that was already removed; the endpoint returns success, the client reloads and shows the member still present or the removal 'succeed' with nothing done — no error distinguishes a real removal from a no-op.
